title: DOL Prevailing Wage Rule Could Price Out Smaller Employers and Immigrants
excerpt: A proposed rule raising H-1B and PERM wage floors by roughly $14,000 per worker per year threatens to shut smaller employers and nonprofits out of the immigration system.
body:
• The Department of Labor's proposed rule would raise prevailing wage floors for H-1B, PERM, and related visa programs, increasing the average certified wage by roughly $14,000 per year per worker.
  • Entry-level wage thresholds would jump from the 17th percentile to the 34th percentile, with proportional increases across all four wage tiers.
  • Smaller employers, nonprofits, and startups that rely on H-1B sponsorship could be shut out of the system if they cannot meet the higher salary requirements.
  • The rule would not apply retroactively to existing prevailing wage determinations or approved Labor Condition Applications, but all new filings would be subject to the higher thresholds once the rule takes effect.

What the Rule Changes

The Department of Labor published a proposed rule in March 2026 that would fundamentally restructure how prevailing wages are calculated for foreign workers sponsored under H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, and PERM labor certification programs. The comment period closed on May 26, and the rule is now moving toward finalization.

At the heart of the proposal is a shift in wage percentile thresholds. Under the current system, the entry-level wage — Level I — is anchored at the 17th percentile of wages in a given occupation and metro area. The DOL's rule would push that floor to the 34th percentile. Level II would move from the 34th to the 52nd percentile, Level III from the 50th to the 70th, and Level IV from the 67th to the 88th.

The DOL estimates these changes would add roughly $6.5 billion in annual wages paid to foreign employees across the economy, according to analysis by immigration law firm Mintz. On a per-worker basis, the average increase works out to about $14,000 per year.

Who Gets Hit Hardest

H-1B employers would constitute the largest affected group, but the ripple effects extend to anyone pursuing employment-based green cards through PERM labor certification for EB-2 and EB-3 categories, as well as employers sponsoring nationals of Chile, Singapore, and Australia under H-1B1 and E-3 visas.

The impact falls disproportionately on smaller employers and nonprofits. As immigration law experts at Cyrus Mehta & Associates noted in their analysis, "by eliminating the current entry-level wage classification and requiring entry-level workers to be offered wages currently at Level II in the OEWS wage system, many smaller employers and nonprofit employers could be shut out of the H-1B and PERM system."

"The proposed rule would require employers to pay a DOL-estimated $6.5 billion in additional annual wages to foreign employees."

— Mintz Immigration Team analysis

Universities, research institutions, and early-stage startups — organizations that routinely hire international talent at entry-level positions — face particularly steep adjustments. A software engineer role in San Francisco that currently qualifies at a Level I wage around $110,000 could see its required floor jump significantly under the new calculations.

The Broader Regulatory Squeeze

The wage rule is one piece of a broader immigration enforcement push. The DOL has also signaled plans to overhaul the PERM labor certification process itself, modernizing how the agency reviews employers' recruitment of qualified U.S. workers. PERM regulations have not been comprehensively updated since 2004, according to the DOL's regulatory agenda.

Meanwhile, the Department of Homeland Security has separately moved to tighten employment authorization for certain visa holders, mandating more frequent renewals and eliminating automatic extensions for pending applications. Bloomberg Law reported that tens of thousands of immigrant workers could be forced out of their jobs as the combined policies take effect.

The Department of Justice has also relaunched its Protecting U.S. Workers Initiative, which investigates employers suspected of discriminating against American workers in favor of foreign hires.

What It Means for Indian Diaspora Workers

Indian nationals are by far the largest group of H-1B visa holders, accounting for roughly 70% of approved petitions in recent years. They also face the longest green card backlogs — often decades — through the EB-2 and EB-3 categories that PERM certifications feed into.

Higher wage floors could cut both ways. Workers already employed at competitive salaries may benefit from stronger wage protections. But those in the early stages of their careers, or working at smaller firms willing to sponsor them, may find fewer employers able or willing to meet the new thresholds.

The rule would not apply retroactively. Previously approved prevailing wage determinations, Labor Condition Applications, and PERM certifications remain unaffected. H-1B cap petitions for fiscal year 2027, which had to be filed by June 30, 2026, are also expected to be grandfathered in under the old wage levels.

What Comes Next

With the public comment period closed, the DOL is now reviewing feedback before issuing a final rule. The timeline for finalization has not been announced. Immigration attorneys widely expect legal challenges once the rule is published, though the DOL's use of standard notice-and-comment rulemaking — rather than the expedited process attempted in 2020 — gives the agency a stronger procedural foundation to defend the changes in court.

Private wage surveys, which some employers use as an alternative to government wage data, remain available under the proposed rule, though the DOL has indicated it will scrutinize their use more closely going forward.
